![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13930904/assets/67b77d2d3798e87593c7dddeea93603fff36d9153f53248cc2dab295f4879321.png)

The figure above shows the graph of $f(x).$ Find ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)}.$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the two functions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(p(x)\cdot q(x)) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-20{x}^{6}\cdot \frac{1}{5{x}^{4}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }((-20\cdot \frac{1}{5})\frac{{x}^{6}}{{x}^{4}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-4{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{2}$ is an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}=\infty .
$$

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient $-4$ causes $y=-4{x}^{2}$ to be a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-4{x}^{2})=-{lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2})=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$
